xrefcode.com / docs / cli / live-memscan

$ xref live memscan

by Alexander Panasenko · xrefcode.com
On this page
  1. Usage
  2. Arguments and options
  3. Examples
  4. A text in the input buffer
  5. Reading the output
  6. Limits
  7. Provenance

Search a running process for a known value: xref scans its private writable memory (rw-p: heap, anonymous mappings, writable data) for consecutive little-endian u64 values and prints the words around each hit. Use it to locate a structure you know a field of, then resolve the pointers next to it with resolve.

Usage

xref live memscan [OPTIONS] --pid <PID> <VALUES>...

Arguments and options

Arguments

<VALUES>...
Consecutive u64 values (0x... hex or decimal) encoded as little-endian bytes.

Options

--pid <PID>
Target process ID (must be non-zero).
--align <ALIGN>
Required byte alignment for matches (1, 2, 4, or 8).
default 8
--before-words <BEFORE_WORDS>
Number of 8-byte words to read before each match (0..=16).
default 2
--after-words <AFTER_WORDS>
Number of 8-byte words to read after each match (0..=16).
default 6
--max-hits <MAX_HITS>
Maximum number of hits before stopping (1..=1024).
default 32
--max-bytes <MAX_BYTES>
Maximum scannable region bytes read before stopping.
default 268435456
--timeout-ms <TIMEOUT_MS>
Cooperative inter-chunk elapsed-time budget in milliseconds.
default 5000
--force-bin
Continue even if --bin does not match /proc/<pid>/exe.
--json
Emit structured schema_version: 1 JSON output.

Examples

The target is ripgrep 14.1.1 (rg) filtering an endless input stream, as on live maps. PIDs and runtime addresses belong to that run.

A text in the input buffer

The eight bytes haystack read as a little-endian u64 are 0x6b63617473796168:

Command
$ sudo xref -b rg live memscan --pid 4084848 0x6b63617473796168 --max-hits 2
Output

Reading the output

  • The second line is the scan summary: the needle as stored in memory, the alignment, how many regions and bytes were read, and why the scan stopped (max_hits, max_bytes, the time budget, or the end of memory).
  • Each hit gives the runtime address and the region it is in; the rows under it are the words before and after (* marks the hit), each with its address, value and a classification: scalar, or a pointer into the binary, heap or stack.

Limits

  • Reading another process's memory needs ptrace access: same user with Yama ptrace_scope 0, the target's permission, or root. This recording used sudo.
  • The scan is a snapshot; memory can change while it runs.

Provenance

Recorded with a development build of xref after 0.4.0 on Linux x86-64, on rg = ripgrep 14.1.1 (official stripped release). Live examples ran against one ripgrep process filtering an endless input stream; commands shown with sudo ran as root. Output is unchanged except that whitespace at the end of each line and empty lines at the end of the output are removed; long outputs are cut where marked.
